description: Classes, objects, and constructors — the blueprint and the house.

screens.body:
A class is a blueprint — it describes what something IS and what it can DO, but it isn't the thing itself. An object is one actual house built from that blueprint. One Dog class, a hundred Dog objects.

Everything in Java lives inside a class. There are no free-floating functions like in JavaScript — even main lives inside a class.

Thinking in blueprints-and-houses makes the rest of OOP click: fields are the house's features, methods are what the house can do, constructors are the construction crew.

options: One instance built from a class

screens.heading: Blueprint vs house
screens.keyPoint: Class = blueprint. Object = the built thing.

screens.heading: Fields: the data a class holds
screens.keyPoint: Fields = the object's data; private by default.

screens.body:
A constructor is the special method that runs when you create an object. It sets the starting values: new Dog("Rex", 3) builds a dog named Rex, age 3.

Constructors have two strict rules: same name as the class, and NO return type — not even void. That absence is how Java knows it's a constructor.

Inside, this.name = name means 'the object's field name gets the parameter name.' The this keyword points at the object being built.

check.question: What must a constructor NOT have?

screens.heading: Constructors build the object
screens.keyPoint: Same name as the class, no return type.

code.snippet:
Dog d = new Dog("Rex"); // d is a reference to the object
d.bark();                  // use the reference to call methods

screens.heading: `new` brings objects to life
screens.keyPoint: new creates the object; the variable holds a reference.

screens.body:
Methods are functions that belong to a class. Instance methods run on a specific object and can freely use its fields: d.bark() can read d's name.

A method declares its return type (or void) and its parameter types, just like the static methods you saw in the basics lesson. The only difference: instance methods don't say static.

Calling one: object.method(arguments). The object before the dot is the one whose data the method works with.

check.question: An instance method like bark() can use…

screens.heading: Methods: what objects can do
screens.keyPoint: Instance methods use the object's own fields.

screens.body:
Encapsulation means hiding an object's insides and exposing only safe ways to interact. Fields stay private; public methods called getters and setters control access.

Why bother? A setter can validate: setAge(-5) can be rejected, while a public field would accept anything. You get to change the internal rules later without breaking everyone's code.

Naming convention: getName() returns the field, setName(...) updates it. IDEs can generate these for you — you'll rarely hand-write them.
screens.heading: Encapsulation: getters and setters

screens.body:
Instance members belong to each object — every Dog has its own name. static members belong to the class itself — one shared copy, no object needed.

You already used static: Math.max(3, 7) calls a static method on the Math class, and main is static because the JVM calls it before any objects exist.

Rule of thumb: if it needs an object's data, make it instance. If it's a utility that stands alone (convert, compute, create), static is fine.

check.question: A static method is called on…

screens.heading: static vs instance
screens.keyPoint: static = on the class. Instance = on each object.
